content.thinking:
The revert at 18:41:45 actually worked, briefly dropping the service to 0.5% at 18:42, but the flag kept flipping back on afterward (18:43, 18:46, 18:52), so the mitigation got marked REFUTED simply because the service wasn't at baseline when checked. The real issue was that something kept re-enabling the monthly-spend-feature flag after it was toggled on at 18:36, exposing the underlying problem.

For impact, I'll stick with the measured 0.30 hour lower bound, 20.1% average error rate against a 1.0% baseline, and a 39.5% peak — not the 0.21h figure. I'll note the uncertainty around who or what kept re-enabling the flag, and that the incident appeared unresolved as of the last metrics read.

For the executive summary, I'll avoid naming internal components directly and instead describe things like "the shop's account page" and "a newly switched-on feature."

assumptions: The outage duration and all impact figures are lower bounds: the service was still failing at the last minute of metrics read, so the true totals are larger than stated.
The 0.21 hours Argus held the incident measures the automated response window only, not how long the service was broken.
Impact is assumed to be confined to account-page requests, because that is the only request type appearing in the error logs; other endpoints were not separately verified.
Why the flag was re-enabled after each revert (another automation, a scheduled rollout, or a human) was not determined from the data available - it is assumed to be an external actor, not Argus.
The conclusion that the faulty code was already deployed and merely gated by the flag rests on the rollback failing for lack of a prior revision; no code diff was inspected.

Argus judged its flag revert REFUTED because the service was not at baseline when it checked; the logs suggest the revert did work while it held, so the REFUTED verdict is treated here as a measurement artefact of the flag being flipped on again rather than evidence against the flag as the cause.
input.executive_summary: Starting at 18:36 UTC on 6 October 2026, the account page of the online shop began failing for a large share of shoppers who loaded it. A newly switched-on feature introduced a crash in the code that builds the monthly spend summary, so requests that hit it returned an error instead of the page. During the failure the error rate averaged 20.1% of traffic against a normal level of 1.0%, peaking at 39.5% - roughly 19.1% of traffic failed that otherwise would have succeeded. Failures came and went with the feature being switched on and off, so the experience for shoppers alternated between normal and heavily degraded. The automated responder detected the alert within about five minutes and switched the feature back off, which restored normal service for as long as it stayed off; however, the feature was turned back on again several times afterwards, so the fix did not hold. An attempt to roll the service back to its previous version failed because no earlier version existed to return to, and the incident was escalated to humans at 18:54 UTC. The service had not recovered by the last minute of data available, so the outage lasted at least 0.30 hours (18 minutes) - that is a lower bound, not a final measurement, and every impact figure above is bounded the same way.
input.root_cause: The `monthly-spend-feature` flag was switched from off to on at 18:36, exposing a code path (`src/io_shop/spend_summary.py:47`) that raises ZeroDivisionError on account-page requests; the error rate tracked the flag state minute-by-minute (30-40% while on, ~0.5-1% baseline noise while off, and an intermediate rate during the 51/149 partial-evaluation minute at onset). The defect was already present in the running revision - the flag only gated its exposure - and the flag was repeatedly flipped back on after Argus reverted it, so the service never stayed recovered.
